title: Ultrasound around the airway: stomach, tube, lungs and diaphragm
summary: Four quick scans around intubation and ventilation: is the stomach full, is the tube in the trachea, are both lungs ventilated, and is the diaphragm working? Learn what each scan answers, and what it cannot.
author: Dr Firas Abou-Auda, Consultant in Emergency Medicine and Course Director, Wavelength
conflicts: Dr Firas Abou-Auda is Course Director of Wavelength, which runs paid ultrasound courses.
audience: Emergency, acute, critical care and anaesthetic doctors, advanced clinical practitioners and physician associates involved in sedation, intubation or ventilation.
outcomes: Classify gastric contents as empty, clear fluid or solid, and use the result in the aspiration-risk assessment
Identify tracheal and oesophageal intubation on neck ultrasound, alongside waveform capnography
Use lung sliding and the lung pulse to detect main bronchus intubation and pneumothorax after intubation
Assess diaphragm movement and recognise weakness or paralysis
Document airway ultrasound findings and their limits
references: Van de Putte P, Perlas A. Ultrasound assessment of gastric content and volume. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 2014.
